title: The Winning of Kinghood: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How Arthur Performed the Miracle of the Sword Twice in Front of Sir Ector, and How the Truth About His Birth Was Revealed to Him._

So Arthur hurried to the part of the lists where Sir Ector sat with the people of his household. He stood before his father and said, “Sir, my brother Kay sent me here to ask you to come at once to the pavilion where we are staying. Truly, I think something very strange has happened, because my brother Kay has a look on his face that I have never seen before.”

Sir Ector wondered greatly why Sir Kay would leave the fighting and call for him at such a time. So he got up from his seat and went with Arthur. They walked to the pavilion, and when he arrived, he saw Sir Kay standing in the middle of it. Sir Ector saw that his son’s face was as white as wood ashes and that his eyes shone with a strange brightness. Sir Ector said, “My son, what is wrong?” Sir Kay answered, “Sir, here is something truly wonderful.” With that, he took his father by the hand and led him to the table that stood in the pavilion. A cloak lay on the table, and something was wrapped inside it. Then Sir Kay opened the cloak, and there lay the sword of the anvil! Both its hilt and its blade gleamed with dazzling splendor.

Sir Ector knew that sword at once, and he knew where it had come from. He was so astonished that he did not know what to do. For a while he could not speak. Then at last he found his voice and cried out loudly, “What is this that I see before me!”
Sir Kay answered, “Sir, I have the sword that stood a short while ago in the anvil, on the block of marble before the great cathedral. So I ask you to tell me what this means.”
Then Sir Ector said, “How did you come by that sword?”
For a while Sir Kay was silent. Then he said, “Sir, I broke my sword in the battle I fought just now, and so I found this sword to use in its place.”

Sir Ector was utterly bewildered and hardly knew whether to believe what he had heard. After a while he said, “If you really drew this sword out of the anvil, then you must be the rightful King of Britain, for that is what the writing on the sword declares. But if you truly drew it out of the anvil, then you will be just as able to push it back into the place you took it from.”

At this, Sir Kay was deeply troubled, and he cried out loudly, “Who could do such a thing? Who could work so great a miracle as to thrust a sword into solid iron?” Sir Ector answered, “That miracle is no greater than the one you worked in drawing it out. Who ever heard of a man who could pull a sword out of a place and yet could not put it back where he found it?”

Sir Kay did not know what to say to his father, and he was afraid that he would not be able to work that miracle. Still, he tried to comfort himself, saying, “If my young brother Arthur could work this miracle, why should I not do the same? Surely I am no less worthy than he is. If he drew the sword out so easily, perhaps I can push it back just as easily.” So he took what comfort he could from these thoughts.

Then he wrapped the sword in the cloak again. He and Sir Ector left the pavilion and made their way to the marble stone and the anvil in front of the cathedral. Arthur went along with his father and his brother, and they did not forbid him. When they came to the place where the sword had been, Sir Kay climbed onto the block of marble and looked at the top of the anvil. The top of the anvil was perfectly smooth, without a single scratch or mark. Sir Kay said to himself, “What is my father asking me to do! Who in all the world could push a sword blade into a solid iron anvil?” But he could not back out of that impossible task. He was forced to try the miracle, so he set the point of the sword against the iron and pressed on it with all his strength. But he could not do it. He struggled with all his might, pressing the sword against the anvil, yet he did not pierce the iron even as deep as the width of a hair.
After he had tried for a long while, he finally gave up and came down from where he stood. He said to his father, “Sir, no man alive can work that miracle.”
Sir Ector answered, “How is it possible, then, that you could have pulled out that sword as you say, and yet you cannot put it back?”

Then young Arthur spoke up and said, “Father, may I speak?” Sir Ector said, “Speak, my son.” Arthur said, “I would like to try holding that sword.” Sir Ector replied, “By what right would you hold that sword?” Arthur said, “Because I was the one who drew that sword out of the anvil for my brother. And as you say, drawing it out is no harder than pushing it back in. So I believe I can set it back into the iron it came from.”

Then Sir Ector looked at young Arthur so strangely that Arthur did not know why he was staring at him that way. So he cried out, “Sir, why do you look at me so strangely? Are you angry with me?” Sir Ector answered, “Before God, my son, I am not angry with you.” Then he said, “If you wish to hold the sword, you may certainly try that miracle.”

So Arthur took the sword from his brother Kay and leaped up onto the marble stone. He set the point of the sword on the anvil and pressed down hard. And the sword slid smoothly into the middle of the anvil until it stood halfway in, and there it held fast. After he had worked that miracle, he drew the sword out again quickly and easily, and then he pushed it back in once more, just as he had done before.

When Sir Ector saw what Arthur had done, he cried out in a very loud voice, “Lord! Lord! What a miracle my eyes have seen!” And when Arthur came down from the block of marble, Sir Ector knelt before him and pressed his hands together, palm to palm.
When Arthur saw what his father was doing, he cried out like someone in great pain, and he said, “Father! Father! Why are you kneeling to me?”

Sir Ector answered him, “I am not your father. Now it is clear that you are surely of very noble birth and that the blood of kings runs in your veins. Otherwise you could not have handled that sword as you have.”
Then Arthur began to weep uncontrollably, and he cried out in deep anguish, “Father! Father! What are you saying? Please get up and do not kneel to me.”
So Sir Ector rose from his knees and stood facing Arthur. He said, “Arthur, why are you weeping?” And Arthur said, “Because I am afraid.”
All this time Sir Kay had stood close by, unable to move or speak. He stood like a man in a trance, and he said to himself, “What is this? Is my brother a King?”
Then Sir Ector spoke. He said, “Arthur, the time has come for you to know who you are, for the true story of your life has been kept hidden from you until now.

“I will confess everything to you. Eighteen years ago a man came to me who was very wise and highly favored by Uther-Pendragon, and that man was the Enchanter Merlin. Merlin showed me the signet ring of Uther-Pendragon. By the power of that ring, he ordered me to be at a certain place at a certain time that he named. The place was the back gate of Uther-Pendragon’s castle, and the time was midnight of that very day.
“He ordered me to tell no one anything about what he told me, and I kept his secret as he asked.

“So I went to that back gate at midnight, as Merlin had commanded. There Merlin came to me with another man, and the other man was Sir Ulfius, the chief knight of Uther-Pendragon’s household. I tell you that these two men were closer to Uther-Pendragon than any other men in the world.

“When those two came up to me, I saw that Merlin was carrying something in his arms, wrapped in a scarlet mantle of fine cloth. He opened the folds of the mantle, and there I saw a newborn child wrapped in swaddling clothes. I saw the child by the light of a lantern that Sir Ulfius carried. He was very fair of face and large of bone—and you were that child.

“Then Merlin gave me my orders. I was to take the child and raise him as my own. He said the child was to be named Arthur, and that no one in all the world was to know anything except that the child was mine. I told Merlin I would do as he wished, and I took the child and carried him home with me. I announced that the child was my own, and everyone believed my words, so no one ever knew anything except that you were my own son. The lady who was my wife took that secret with her to Paradise when she died. Since then, until now, no one in the world has known about this matter except me and those two men I told you of.

“Until now I have never known who your father was. But now I suspect who he was, and that you have very high and kingly blood in your veins. I think that perhaps your father was Uther-Pendragon himself. For who but the son of Uther-Pendragon could have drawn that sword out of the anvil as you have?”

When Arthur heard his father say this, he cried out in a loud and violent voice, “Woe! Woe! Woe!” He said those words three times. Sir Ector said, “Arthur, why are you so sorrowful?” And Arthur said, “Because I have lost my father, and I would rather have my father than be a King!”

While these things were happening, two men came to that place. They were very tall and had a noble and proud bearing. When the two men came near, Arthur, Sir Ector and Sir Kay saw that one of them was the Enchanter Merlin and the other was Sir Ulfius. Both men were famous and well known all over the world. When the two had reached the three, Merlin said, “How goes it?” Sir Ector answered, “It goes in a most wonderful way. Look, Merlin! This is the child you brought to me eighteen years ago, and you can see that he has grown into a man.”

Then Merlin said, “Sir Ector, I know very well who this young man is, for I have watched over him carefully all this time. I know that Britain’s hope lies in him. Moreover, I tell you that even today, in the surface of an enchanted mirror, I have seen everything he has done since morning. I know how he drew the sword from the anvil and how he pushed it back in. I know how he drew it out and pushed it back a second time. I also know everything you have been telling him just now, and so I declare that you have told him the plain truth. And now the spirit of prophecy is upon me, and I can see into the future. You, Arthur, will become the greatest and most famous King who ever lived in Britain. I see that many knights of extraordinary excellence will gather around you, and that men will tell of their marvelous deeds as long as this land lasts. I see that through these knights your reign will be full of splendor and glory. I see that the most marvelous adventure of the Holy Grail will be achieved by three of the knights of your Court. This will bring you lasting fame, for you will be the King in whose reign the holy cup is won. All these things I foresee. And now the time is near when the glory of your House will be shown to the world again, and all the people of this land will rejoice in you and your kingship. So, Sir Ector, for these next three days, I charge you to guard this young man as the apple of your eye, for the hope and safety of this whole realm lie in him.”

Then Sir Ector raised his voice and cried to Arthur, “A boon! A boon!” Arthur said, “Alas! What is this? Do you, my father, ask a boon of me? I can give you anything in the world that is mine. Ask what you wish, and it is yours!” Then Sir Ector said, “I beg this of you: that when you are King, your brother Kay may be Seneschal of this whole realm.” Arthur said, “It shall be as you ask.” And he said, “As for you, it shall be better still, for you shall be my father until the end!” With these words, he took Sir Ector’s head in his hands and kissed him on the forehead and on both cheeks, and so he sealed his promise.

All this while Sir Kay had stood as if struck by thunder. He did not know whether to be lifted to the skies or cast down into the depths, because his young brother had passed him by and been raised to such an astonishing height of fortune. So he stood like someone who had lost all life and movement.

Let it be said here that Arthur kept everything he had promised his father. In later times he made Sir Kay his Seneschal, and Sir Ector was a father to him until the day he died, which happened five years after this.
That is how the royal blood of Arthur first came to light. Now listen, and you will hear how it was proved to the whole world.
